topIssues.title: Game-proving retries discard completed proofs and regenerate all witnesses
topIssues.author: Inphi
topIssues.body:
## Summary

The proposer does not checkpoint progress while proving a multi-chunk game. If any chunk fails,
the entire game-proving attempt fails and all successful chunk results held in memory are
discarded. The defense scheduler then retries the unresolved game from the beginning, regenerating
the same witnesses and requesting the same SPN proofs again.

This can discard proofs that SPN has already fulfilled and charged for. It also repeats expensive
local witness generation and can prevent a defense from making progress when one transient or
persistent error occurs late in the range.

This is related to, but distinct from, https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/22621. This issue also affects chunks whose proofs were fully fulfilled,
downloaded, and validated before a different chunk failed.

## Current behavior

Each game is split into chunks. A chunk generates and validates its local outputs and, when using
the network provider, obtains both a range proof and a consolidation proof. Successful
`ChunkResult` values remain only in memory while the proposer waits for every chunk:

```rust
let results: Vec<ChunkResult> = futures::stream::iter(tasks)
    .buffer_unordered(max_concurrent)
    .try_collect()
    .await?;
```

`try_collect()` returns immediately when any chunk produces an error. Previously completed
`ChunkResult` values are dropped along with any other in-flight futures. The caller reports the
game-proving task as failed.

Because the disputed game still requires a defense, the scheduler starts another game-proving
task. The new task has no record of completed chunks or fulfilled proof IDs, so it:

1. derives the game span again;
2. regenerates witnesses for every chunk;
3. resubmits proof requests for work that may already have been fulfilled; and
4. discards everything again if any chunk in the new attempt fails.

There is no durable per-game progress record, completed-chunk cache, or proof-artifact recovery
path.

## Impact

- Fulfilled and paid-for SPN proofs can be unused.
- Identical proof work can be requested and charged more than once.
- Local witness generation repeatedly consumes CPU and memory.
- A failure in one chunk invalidates progress made by every other chunk.
- Persistent submission failures can create an unbounded retry loop that recomputes identical
  witnesses without advancing the defense.
- Repeated full retries increase the risk of missing the dispute-game response window.

The cost grows with the split count and with how late in an attempt the first failure occurs.

## Example failure sequence

1. A game is divided into multiple chunks.
2. Several chunks finish witness generation and receive both required proofs from SPN.
3. A later chunk encounters a transient RPC, submission, balance, or proving error.
4. `try_collect()` returns that error and drops all completed chunk results.
5. The game-proving task exits without producing the aggregation proof or submitting the defense.
6. The scheduler retries the same game from scratch.
7. Already-completed witnesses and proofs are regenerated and requested again.

## Expected behavior

Successful chunk work should survive an unrelated chunk failure. A retry should resume from the
incomplete or failed chunks and reuse completed results after validating that they belong to the
same immutable proving inputs.

At minimum, an in-process retry should not regenerate fulfilled chunks. Ideally, progress should
also survive proposer restarts.

## Suggested regression test

Use a mock witness generator and proof provider with at least two chunks:

- Chunk A completes and returns both proofs.
- Chunk B returns an error after A has completed.
- Invoke the same game-proving operation again.

Assert that chunk A's witnesses and proof requests are not generated a second time, while chunk B
is retried. Also assert that changing any input that affects proof validity invalidates the cached
result.

## Possible fix direction

Represent game-proving progress explicitly instead of keeping it solely in the `try_collect()`
call. Record each completed chunk and each submitted proof request against a stable attempt
identity containing the inputs required to determine safe reuse, such as the game claim, prestate
or verifying keys, chunk boundaries, and relevant chain inputs.

On retry, validate the recorded identity, restore completed chunks, recover or poll submitted
proof IDs, and schedule only missing work. Before returning an attempt-level error, retain or
explicitly clean up all externally submitted requests.

Changing fail-fast collection alone may prevent immediate cancellation of sibling futures, but it
does not provide recovery after the task exits or the process restarts. The proof-request lifecycle
and completed-chunk lifecycle need explicit ownership.

topIssues.title: opgeth-decoupling: own the log layer — op-service/log becomes the monorepo logging API
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
Part of #21745 (§15 of the [op-geth decoupling doc](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/1657fbe391d3f37785a6a3609422ee79fe86d9fa/docs/ai/opgeth-decoupling.md#L416-L436)). **Blocks #20266.**

`op-service/log` becomes the monorepo's logging API: no monorepo Go file imports `go-ethereum/log`. This is better layering regardless of the decoupling — the fork's `Logger.SetContext`/`WriteCtx`/`LogAttrs`/`Trace…ErrorContext` extensions are just what forces it.

## Scope (measured at 1657fbe)

- **697** monorepo Go files import `github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/log` — op-node 121, op-service 82, op-challenger 71, op-e2e 65, op-dispute-mon 48, op-test-sequencer 42, op-devstack 37, op-chain-ops 36, op-deployer 33, op-supernode 27, op-batcher 21, op-conductor 20, and a long tail. (`superchain-registry/` is a submodule with its own Go module — out of scope, flagged to that team.)
- **63** of those import *both* `geth/log` and `oplog`, so they need symbol-level dedup, not a blind import rewrite.
- Only ~13 files use the fork's context extensions at all: [`op-service/testlog`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/1657fbe391d3f37785a6a3609422ee79fe86d9fa/op-service/testlog/testlog.go), [`op-service/log/logfilter`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/tree/1657fbe391d3f37785a6a3609422ee79fe86d9fa/op-service/log/logfilter), `op-service/tls/tlsinfo.go`, `op-devstack/devtest`, plus a handful of call sites. Phase 2 is therefore small; phase 1 is the bulk.

## PRs

1. **`op-service/log`: add the `oplog` logger surface.** `type Logger = log.Logger` (alias) plus re-exports of the package-level API actually in use: `New`, `NewLogger`, `Root`, `SetDefault`, `With`, `Info/Warn/Error/Debug/Trace/Crit`, the `Level*`/`Lvl*` constants, `LevelFromString`, `FromLegacyLevel`, `DiscardHandler`, `NewTerminalHandler[WithLevel]`, `JSONHandler`, `LogfmtHandlerWithLevel`, `Handler`. Migrate `op-service` itself as the first consumer.
2. **Tree-wide sweep + gate.** Rewrite the remaining ~615 files to `oplog`, dedup the 63 dual-import files, and add a lint/CI gate (golangci `depguard`, or a grep check) that fails any new `go-ethereum/log` import. Pure rename while the alias holds — zero behaviour change; build + test is the gate. Land fast to avoid rebase churn against everything in flight.
3. **Flip the alias to an owned interface** *(at cutover)*. Replace the alias with an interface — upstream's method set plus the context methods — over an `slog`-backed implementation. Do **not** copy upstream's LGPL `log` package; the context-extension logic is OP-authored and ports over. Our interface is a superset of upstream's, so an `oplog.Logger` still satisfies `log.Logger` wherever we hand one into geth code (e.g. the in-process L1 geth in op-e2e).

PRs 1–2 land now and are independent of the rest of the epic. PR 3 lands with or just before the go.mod flip.

## Acceptance criteria

- No monorepo Go file imports `go-ethereum/log`, enforced by a CI/lint gate.
- `op-service/log/logfilter` and `op-service/testlog` build on the owned API with unchanged behaviour.
- After PR 3, `op-service/log` has no `go-ethereum/log` dependency, and an `oplog.Logger` is still accepted by geth APIs taking `log.Logger`.

topPRs.title: feat: add private interop cleanroom implementation
topPRs.author: opsuperchain
topPRs.body:
## Summary

- add the private-interop private/rendering chain pair, contracts, deterministic rendering codec, builder, and claim-follow path
- integrate the pair with op-deployer, op-batcher, op-supernode, op-interop-filter, devstack, and op-up
- add private-pair-aware interop smoke coverage and a design document
- harden the implementation after adversarial review: structurally close deposits, bind rendering inputs and emitters, cap amplification, remove the separate operator key/premine, disable the stock ETH path, and make rendering execution fully zero-fee

## `op-up --private-interop` topology

```text
                         L1 EL + beacon node
                          ^              |
                          | batches      | derives
         +----------------+---+      +---v-----------------+
         |                    |      |                     |
   normal A batcher    private-interop batcher       shared supernode
         ^                    ^                      public view: {A, B-render}
         |                    |                         |          |
 A sequencer op-node   B private op-node               |          |
         |                    |                         |          |
 A sequencer op-reth   B private op-reth         A verifier   B rendering
   public chain 901    private chain 902           op-reth       op-reth
                              ^                                     |
                              +------ `/902/claimed` ----------------+
```

- Chain A is an ordinary public OP chain with a stock batcher and proposer.
- Chain B has two different histories sharing chain ID 902: the sequenced, user-facing custom-gas-token private chain and a public, derived-only rendering with no sequencer or mempool.
- The private-interop batcher reads private B blocks, converts exported logs into claim/replay transactions, checks the rendering parent, and posts an ordinary channel to L1.
- The shared supernode derives and judges `{A, B-render}` using the stock message database and cross-safety logic. It has no private-chain access and does not know that B is a rendering.
- The only private-interop addition in the supernode is the `/902/claimed` follow endpoint. It reconstructs the committed private-B safe block reference from public rendering claims for the private op-node; it does not alter judging.
- Private B and rendering B are never P2P-peered: they deliberately have the same chain ID but different genesis hashes and block contents.
- `--smoke` runs `interopsmoke` in the same process so private receipt positions can be resolved to their canonical public rendering positions.

## Verification

- `go test ./op-batcher/batcher ./op-chain-ops/interopsmoke/... ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/state ./op-interop-filter/filter ./op-private-interop/... ./op-supernode/supernode/chain_container -count=1`
- focused op-deployer private-interop genesis/rollup integration tests
- 49/49 private-interop Solidity tests
- 24/24 L2-to-L2 messenger Solidity tests
- 15/15 L2 genesis Solidity tests
- `op-up --private-interop --smoke`: chain identity, native transfers, valid messages in both directions, rendered private-chain message resolution, and invalid-message reorg all pass

## Notes

This is intentionally a draft for design and security review. The stock Superchain ETH bridge smoke case is skipped on the custom-gas-token private half; that path is closed by design and `NativeMintBridge` is the sanctioned liquidity path.

topPRs.title: private-interop: derive public projection from one genesis
topPRs.author: karlfloersch
topPRs.body:
## Summary

This carries forward the private interop implementation from #22720, but replaces the draft's two-role/two-deployer genesis flow with one source of truth:

- op-deployer emits one private-chain genesis and rollup config; there is no public/rendering deployer role
- `ProjectGenesisFrom(privateChainGenesis)` is a pure, deterministic local transform with independent Go and Rust implementations and a shared cross-language golden vector
- op-reth accepts the same private genesis and applies the projection before database initialization with `--rollup.private[=true]`; the private EL consumes it unchanged
- op-batcher and op-supernode detect `private_interop` from the private rollup config, load the local private genesis, and derive the public projection automatically
- the projected state restores stock ETH semantics, installs the replay/claim predeploys, removes private-only liquidity/mint machinery, and clears only the private-chain feature bit
- private interop derives an L1 resource configuration with `maxResourceLimit = 0`, closing deposits through the stock portal rather than a custom L1 contract
- old role flags, compatibility paths, configurable projection predeploy addresses, and the second op-deployer run are deleted

The remainder of #22720 is retained: claim/replay contracts and codec, deterministic batch construction, claim-follow routing, interop-filter integration, devstack/op-up wiring, and acceptance coverage.

## Deployment shape

1. Run op-deployer once with the chain's `privateInterop` stanza and custom gas token configuration.
2. Give the emitted genesis to the private op-reth normally.
3. Give that same genesis to the public-projection op-reth with `--rollup.private=true`.
4. Give the private genesis path to op-batcher and op-supernode; their private-interop paths activate from the rollup marker and derive the matching projection locally.
5. Give the private LightCL the ordinary private-chain genesis/config. It follows the supernode's `/claimed` route as in #22720.

No projection step performs a network call. The embedded implementation bytecode is checked against the current contracts artifacts in the op-deployer integration test.

## Verification

- `go test ./op-private-interop/...`
- `go test ./op-batcher/batcher ./op-batcher/flags`
- `go test ./op-supernode/cmd ./op-supernode/supernode/...`
- `go test ./op-interop-filter/... ./op-node/rollup`
- focused op-deployer private-interop integration, pipeline, and state tests
- `go test ./op-devstack/sysgo -run '^$'`
- `cargo test -p reth-optimism-chainspec private_interop` (4/4)
- `cargo test -p reth-optimism-node private` (1/1)
- `just lint` in contracts-bedrock
- messenger Solidity suite (24/24)

The broad op-deployer pipeline package also ran locally; its only failures were nine live-Sepolia tests that require `SEPOLIA_RPC_URL`. The focused private-interop tests pass.

## Review note

A manual deletion/configuration review was completed, including a differential comparison against the retired two-deployer genesis path. Automated sub-agent review was unavailable in this harness.

topPRs.title: kona: Add in-process zkVM canary for kona-sp1
topPRs.author: Inphi
topPRs.body:
## Overview

Adds `kona-zkvm-canary`, a long-running service that continuously executes the published Kona `super-range` guest against finalized live-network inputs using SP1’s CPU executor.

The canary executes both range and consolidation modes, compares their outputs with the native results produced during witness collection, and reports correctness failures without generating proofs or submitting work to the Succinct Prover Network.

This service is analogous to the vm-runner (op-challenger runner).

## What changed

- Added a finalized snapshot source that:
  - selects consecutive finalized timestamps;
  - pins L1 at `min(CurrentL1 - 1, L1 finalized)`;
  - validates super-root proofs, chain coverage, safety horizons, and span linkage;
  - resolves reported L1 identities against the configured L1 RPC;
  - classifies malformed or inconsistent parent data as `input_error`.
- Added in-process, sequential SP1 execution for range and consolidation modes.
- Added explicit SP1 cycle and memory limits.
  - Cycle-limit exhaustion is reported as `cycle_limit_exceeded`, never as a guest rejection.
  - The wall-clock deadline covers cancellable selection and witness stages only.
- Added fingerprint-based scheduling:
  - successful fingerprints are not rerun;
  - correctness failures receive one confirmation attempt;
  - attempts never overlap and cadence starts after completion.
- Added graceful shutdown during cancellable stages. A signal during uncancellable SP1 execution
  terminates the process and leaves restart handling to the orchestrator.
- Added startup artifact authentication:
  - loads `<prestate>.range.bin.gz`;
  - bounds compressed and decompressed sizes;
  - verifies the decompressed ELF SHA-256 and SP1 verification key;
  - keeps the authenticated ELF entirely in memory.
- Added structured, credential-redacted logging.
- Added Prometheus metrics for lifecycle, outcomes, target progress, stage durations, aggregate SP1 reports, artifact identity, and process memory.
  - Per-phase cycle and invocation totals remain in structured report logs rather than Prometheus series.
- Added `--once` for manual diagnostics using the normal execution path and existing `EXIT_VALID`, `EXIT_INVALID`, and `EXIT_INFRA` conventions.
- Added Melange/APKO packaging and image routing for a non-root, binary-only `kona-zkvm-canary` image. The guest ELF is not embedded in the image.
- Documented configuration, trust boundaries, execution bounds, metrics, and one-shot operation.

## Operational decisions

- Execution is in-process because SP1 already moves emulator work onto Tokio’s blocking pool.
- SP1 execution is not wrapped in a Tokio timeout because `spawn_blocking` work cannot be
  cancelled. The SP1 cycle limit is the resource-reclaiming execution bound.
- Finalized supernode responses are assumed immutable for a timestamp. The selected snapshot stays
  in memory for the attempt and is not fetched again after execution.
- The service writes no files. The sp1-sdk `TRACE_FILE` is rejected during configuration.
- Configuration and artifact authentication complete before the metrics listener is bound.
- `/health` comes from `kona-sp1-host-utils`; no readiness gauge or dedicated readiness behavior
  was added.
- No canary guest execution was added to CI, acceptance tests, or devstack.

Part of #18325

topPRs.title: kona-node,kona-chainview: pilot a SQL chain view compiled by Feldera behind the chainview feature
topPRs.author: teddyknox
topPRs.body:
**Experiment, not a merge proposal.** This is the pilot from a design study on using upstream Feldera (crates.io `dbsp` + the `sql-to-dbsp` compiler, no fork) to replace hand-maintained derived state in kona-node with one incrementally maintained circuit. It is opened as a draft so the delta can be discussed with real code and numbers; the write-up with the reasoning, the reflections, and the proposed next steps is the design study `docs/feldera-in-kona-node.md` in the opql repo (rendered copy: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/a3ea095f-5297-4c98-8841-35f6008f0fe7).

**Why.** kona-node keeps the consequences of chain facts in several places by hand: the safe head is copied into four structures, one L1 poll fans out to three consumers, finality lives in a map that is cleared on every pipeline reset and finalizes by number, `optimism_syncStatus` makes three L1 RPCs per call, and `optimism_safeHeadAtL1Block` is unimplemented. Each copy is a place for a reorg or a reset to leave state behind.

**What changes for an operator.** The chain view is not optional: the paths it replaces are deleted, not gated. Concretely:

- Finality is driven by the chain view's `finalized_l2` view and sent to the engine by hash, guarded to be above the engine's finalized head and at or below the last confirmed safe head. It survives pipeline resets. `L2Finalizer`, the finalized-L1 fan-out to derivation, and finalize-by-number are gone.
- `optimism_syncStatus` serves its L1 fields from the chain view's snapshot with no L1 RPC on the request path; the watcher's three-RPC `L1State` query is gone.
- `optimism_safeHeadAtL1Block` is implemented with op-node's SafeDB semantics (nearest entry at or below the requested L1 block; not persisted across restarts).
- The gossip signer is read from the `SystemConfig` contract at every polled L1 head (one storage read per head) instead of scanned from that head's logs, so a rotation in a skipped block is no longer lost; the watcher's per-chain signer scan is gone.
- The chain view's L1 blocks are the derivation pipeline's own traversal: the derivation actor pushes every origin it advances through, including the heights it re-walks after a reset. There is no separate L1 walk, no window, no backfill at startup, no flag, and no L1 read beyond the signer's. The L1 watcher only polls the head, safe and finalized tags, publishes them on watch channels, and fans heads out to derivation.
- The engine's imported blocks are held by the chain view (the newest 256 at or above the engine's finalized head, pruned as finality advances) and served to derivation's hash-keyed block and `SystemConfig` lookups through a small `ImportedL2Blocks` trait in `kona-providers-alloy`, so that crate and the host binary that depends on it stay free of the chain view. `kona-providers-local`, a 32-block LRU with chain-event and reorg-depth handling that nothing in the node fed, is deleted.

**Size.** Against `develop`, lockfile excluded: the new crate is 2,124 lines (1,754 product including `build.rs` and its README, 370 tests). kona's existing crates gain 752 product and 339 test lines and lose 2,286: the finalizer, the finalized-L1 fan-out, the signer scan, the `L1State` query, `kona-providers-local`, and their tests.

**Reasons a reviewer cannot see in the diff.**

- The SQL program (`crates/node/chainview/src/chainview.sql`) is compiled at build time by Feldera's `sql-to-dbsp` v0.342.0, shipped as a sha256-pinned release JAR that `build.rs` locates but never downloads (`just chainview-fetch-compiler` fetches and verifies it). This adds JDK 21 and the JAR as prerequisites for every `--workspace` / `--all-features` build, so **the Rust CI jobs are expected to fail on this PR** until either the CI image carries both or the crate leaves the default workspace members. That is one of the open questions, not an oversight.
- Every table is a plain Z-set with no primary key: a reorg is a retraction and a status change is a retract-and-insert, so the circuit is never reset. The only command a view drives is the monotone finalize; nothing else asserts what was done.
- The held L2 blocks are host state in the driver, not a table: no view needs a block body, and the driver already tracks the finalized head that prunes them. A SystemConfig fold was built and then removed because nothing consumed it; derivation keeps its own.
- `Engine::reset` now publishes the post-reset state on its watch channel (one line, unconditional). Without it the chain view saw pre-reset heads until the next task.
- The multi-chain watcher keeps its per-chain derivation fan-out and config queries. The view's L1 facts come from each chain's derivation actor, so a multi-chain host would get them per chain; the L1 tag statuses and the signer read are per node for now.
- Reorgs need no code of their own in the view: the pipeline re-walks the heights it rewound over after a reset, and an origin that arrives at a height already held with another hash replaces it and its update rows.

**Validation.** Circuit-level tests through the typed handles (finality, safe-head guard, L1 reorg replacement, reset retraction, nearest-at-or-below lookup, signer rotation and rollback, finalized pruning, the held blocks' cap and pruning, LATENESS drops); host tests for the derivation actor's origin publishing, finalize guard and confirmation pairing, the chain-view actor's tag statuses and signer read, the watcher's fan-out and watches, and the providers wrapper's local-first lookups; clippy `-D warnings` and rustfmt clean. sysgo: a new `TestSafeHeadHistoryMatchesOpNodeSafeDB` compares kona's `safeHeadAtL1Block` history against op-node's SafeDB on a mixed devnet with the DSL's own comparison; it passes on `develop` (24 safe blocks across several L1 blocks, every entry equal), as do the full `node/common` package (one pre-existing skip) and `node/restart`, and all three suites were re-run after each cut, the last one included. `node/reorgs` was not rerun on `develop`; on the original base its one failing subtest failed with the feature off as well. Both nodes' `syncStatus` L1 fields agreed throughout. Not run: a soak, an induced L1 reorg, and a signer rotation on a devnet.

**Found in passing.** Two things worth knowing beyond this PR:

- kona-node enables its Prometheus listener on port 9090 with no metrics flags set, so two kona-nodes on one host collide at startup ("Address already in use"); the parallel sysgo suites need `KONA_METRICS_ENABLED=false`. Not fixed here.
- The global `--metrics.enabled` has clap id `enabled` (its field name), and clap propagates a global argument's explicit value into every subcommand under that id. Any `node` subcommand flag whose field is also named `enabled` is silently overwritten, which is how `KONA_METRICS_ENABLED=false` switched an earlier, optional version of the chain view off during validation. There is no such flag any more, but the trap is live for any future `enabled` field on a subcommand.

**Reviews.** The repo's `rust-code-reviewer` and `go-code-reviewer` guides were applied as two independent review passes before opening. Fixed from them: the finality guard compared numbers only (now also the hash at the safe height, and a reset retracts an equal-height row with another hash); the safe-head history was unbounded (now capped, default 8192 entries); `LATENESS` was unchecked against the chain's `seq_window_size + channel_timeout` (the node now refuses to start when it would drop re-derived rows); the sysgo test hand-rolled the SafeDB walk (now the DSL's `VerifySafeHeadDatabaseMatches`); dead API and unused dependencies. Their findings on the separate canonical L1 walk (re-anchor seed rows, failing closed below the window, retrying transient reads) were fixed and then made moot by removing the walk in favour of the pipeline's traversal; the SystemConfig fold and its per-block log read went with it. Dismissed or deferred: a unit test for the one-line `Engine::reset` publish (no mock engine client exists; it is its own commit instead), hoisting the signer storage-slot read shared with `flags/p2p.rs` (touches unrelated CLI code), and the CI/Java question above, which is the PR's main open point.

topPRs.title: contracts: revive SuperchainTokenBridge + add SuperchainERC20Factory (wrap/unwrap)
topPRs.author: opsuperchain
topPRs.body:
# Description

This PR revives the `SuperchainTokenBridge` and adds a new `SuperchainERC20Factory` that lets any existing ERC20 be wrapped into a `SuperchainERC20` and moved across the Superchain.

## Commit 1: revive the SuperchainTokenBridge

`SuperchainTokenBridge`, `SuperchainERC20`, and `IERC7802` were removed in #19999 (and #20141) as unused interop contracts. This commit restores them from history at their original semvers and predeploy slot (`0x4200...0028`), adapted to the predeploy machinery that has landed since (`Predeploys.getAllRecords()` registry, `L2ContractsManager` deploy/upgrade flow, gate assertions in `L2Genesis`). The bridge is gated behind interop exactly like `SuperchainETHBridge`/`ETHLiquidity`. The legacy `OptimismSuperchainERC20` lane (beacon, factory, `L2StandardBridgeInterop`) is intentionally not revived; the new factory below replaces it.

## Commit 2: SuperchainERC20Factory

A minimal wrap/unwrap factory, added as an interop-gated predeploy at `0x4200...0026` (the slot freed by the old `OptimismSuperchainERC20Factory`):

- `deploy(chainId, token, name, symbol, decimals)` deploys a `SuperchainWrappedERC20` via CREATE2 with `salt = keccak256(chainId, token)`. The wrapped token's constructor takes no arguments (metadata is read back from the factory during construction), so its initcode is constant and **the wrapped token address is identical on every chain**, derived purely from the `[chain_id, address]` identity of the original token.
- On the original token's chain, metadata is read from the token itself (falling back to caller-supplied values for tokens without the metadata extension). On remote chains the deployer supplies it — or, better, uses propagation:
- `propagate(token, toChainId)` sends the canonical wrapped metadata from the token's home chain to the factory on another chain via the `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger` (the factory is the same predeploy address everywhere, mirroring `SuperchainTokenBridge.sendERC20`/`relayERC20`). `relayDeploy` on the destination requires the messenger, the factory itself as cross-domain sender, and **message source chain == the token's claimed home chain**, so remote chains get authentic metadata without trusting any caller.
- `wrap(token, amount)` escrows original tokens in the factory and mints the wrapped token 1:1 (mints the actually-received amount, so fee-on-transfer tokens can't inflate supply beyond backing). Only possible on the token's home chain.
- `unwrap(token, amount)` burns wrapped tokens and releases escrow.
- The wrapped token is a standard `SuperchainERC20`: `crosschainMint`/`crosschainBurn` are gated to the `SuperchainTokenBridge`, so once deployed on two chains, `sendERC20`/`relayERC20` move it between them. Escrow on the home chain always equals global wrapped supply.

## Notes for reviewers

- The revive commit restores the bridge byte-for-byte where possible; the only source adaptations are the solady import path (the versioned `@solady-v0.0.245` remapping no longer exists; the vendored solady is v0.0.158) and registration in the new predeploy registry.
- `L2ContractsManager` semver bumped 1.13.0 → 1.14.0.
- Rebasing tokens are not supported by the wrap/unwrap escrow (negative rebases can strand late unwrappers), same caveat as any escrow wrapper.

## Tests

- Restored `SuperchainTokenBridge` and `SuperchainERC20` unit tests.
- New suites for the factory (deterministic addresses, home/remote metadata, propagate/relayDeploy auth + source-chain checks, wrap/unwrap, fee-on-transfer, escrow accounting) and the wrapped token (factory/bridge mint-burn gating, ERC7802 interface).
